title: Vanern Electronics component buy: 'market price hike' versus an EOL part from an unauthorized broker
scenario_text:
Vanern Electronics needs a critical microcontroller for its flagship product. In the #procurement Slack channel the commodity buyer writes: 'Prices are up and lead times are out - it's the usual silicon market tightness. A distributor has 50,000 units in stock at a premium. I say we place a large buy now to secure supply before it gets worse. It's just market conditions.' Posted Thursday.

Other systems complicate the buy. In the manufacturer's product-change-notification feed, this exact part received an end-of-life notice four months ago with a last-time-buy date already passed. In the approved-vendor list, the 'distributor' offering the 50,000 units is not a franchised/authorized distributor - it is an independent broker. In the quality system, an incoming-inspection ticket from a prior broker lot flagged mismatched date codes and re-marked packages (counterfeit indicators). In the authorized distributor's portal, the part shows 'discontinued - no stock,' making a fresh 50,000-unit availability from a broker implausible for genuine parts. And an engineering note says a pin-compatible successor part is already qualified for the next board revision.

Each signal is individually explainable: silicon markets are tight, brokers do hold legitimate stock, and date-code questions can be benign. But together - a passed EOL last-time-buy, an unauthorized broker as the only source of a large 'in-stock' quantity, prior counterfeit indicators on broker lots, the authorized channel showing discontinued/no-stock, and a qualified successor part available - they point to counterfeit/EOL risk, not a normal market buy. The buyer's 'market conditions' read ignores the PCN and the broker's unauthorized status. You own this commodity. What should you recommend?
question: What should the procurement owner recommend regarding the microcontroller buy?
choices: Place the 50,000-unit buy now from the distributor to secure supply ahead of further market tightening.
Negotiate a lower price with the distributor and place a slightly smaller buy to reduce cost exposure.

Do not place the broker buy; transition to the qualified pin-compatible successor part and, if bridge stock is truly needed, source only through authorized channels with full traceability and counterfeit testing: the passed EOL last-time-buy, unauthorized broker, prior counterfeit indicators, and discontinued authorized stock indicate counterfeit/EOL risk, not market tightness.
Place the buy but route the incoming lot through standard receiving to catch any defects during production.
